detail.abstract: A Time-Based Straddle (TBS) sells an at-the-money call and put at a fixed clock time and closes the position at a later fixed time, at a stop-loss, or at expiry. We develop a unified mathematical treatment of the TBS for an arbitrary number of sessions to expiry and study zero-days-to-expiry (0-DTE) options as its limiting case. Under geometric Brownian motion and Black-Scholes pricing we derive the exact at-the-money straddle value, its square-root time-decay law and the per-session decay share 1-D/(D + 1), and the theta-gamma identity that links premium collection to gamma exposure. We show that the expected P&L of a TBS is the variance risk premium weighted by dollar gamma, give an exact expression for the expected P&L of a straddle held to expiry, and prove that stop-loss and re-entry rules defined on observable prices cannot change expected P&L when implied and realised volatility coincide; they reshape the distribution instead. Monte Carlo experiments calibrated to NIFTY index options quantify these results across 0, 1, 2 and 4 days to expiry and across stop levels. Using one-minute NIFTY weekly option and spot data from November 2023 to May 2025, we find that implied variance exceeds one-minute realised variance at every DTE, but that this premium is offset by trending intraday moves on expiry day and by overnight repricing at longer DTE, so a single clock-driven straddle earns no significant edge before or after costs. Spreading six entries across expiry day, from 09:20 to 14:20, gives a positive mean that is stable in sign across subperiods and cost assumptions but not statistically established. Expiry-day straddles decay faster than the square-root law, and multi-day straddles decay more slowly within the session. The 0-DTE case concentrates premium, decay, gamma and tail risk in a single session, and we discuss the modelling features it requires: total-variance implied volatility, intraday variance seasonality, and jumps.

detail.abstract: Digital microinsurance can widen access to financial protection, yet policyholders may fail to renew because of irregular income, payment friction, limited product understanding, or difficulty obtaining timely assistance. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots may reduce some barriers by explaining policy terms, answering questions conversationally, and providing timely reminders. They may also introduce risks, including inaccurate explanations, privacy concerns, automation bias, and messages perceived as coercive. This paper develops a protocol for a proposed randomised controlled trial (RCT) to evaluate whether a generative AI chatbot improves policy retention in digital microinsurance. The proposed design compares chatbot-supported renewal communication with standard digital communication among eligible policyholders approaching a renewal or contribution deadline. The primary outcome is objectively recorded retention at a prespecified follow-up point; secondary outcomes include payment timeliness, comprehension, service resolution, trust, complaints, and opt-out rates. Randomisation, allocation concealment, intention-to-treat analysis, and consumer safeguards are specified. No participant-level experimental dataset was supplied, so this paper does not report completed trial findings. Instead, it presents a reproducible protocol and analysis plan for implementation following ethics review and data access approval, with relevance to Ghana, Nigeria, and other digital microinsurance markets.

detail.abstract: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford for the microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization, rests on the observation that prices adjust slowly and at staggered intervals. We examine what this implies for the link between hotel class, guest expectations and revenue. Ten hotels from upper midscale to luxury, in six U.S. markets and Spain, supplied 876 online reviews matched to monthly STR market performance. LIWC scored guests’ Achievement, Affiliation and Power language, and structural equation models related motives, seven guest ratings and class to perceived value, RevPAR and ADR. Guests judged value against one quality factor (β = .91), and every hotel showed a value gap, with Value rated on average 0.37 points below the other attributes. The gap narrowed by 0.11 points per class step, so higher class bought guests’ tolerance of price. Within hotels, months of higher market ADR were associated with a wider gap (−0.12 per $100, p ≈ .07), consistent with prices moving while delivered quality stays fixed. The Slutsky decomposition replicated: RevPAR related positively (income effect, β = .96) and occupancy negatively (substitution effect, β = −.28) to ADR. Once markets and guest variables were modeled, class no longer predicted RevPAR, while Power language did (β = .17). Managers should treat the value gap as a signal for resetting rate positions and protect delivered quality before raising rates.

detail.abstract: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences, awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford for the microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization, rests on a simple observation: prices adjust slowly and at staggered intervals. We ask what this implies for hotels, where daily rates move constantly but a property’s rate position against its class tier is reset only occasionally. Building on Tran and Egan’s (2025) attribution model and on recent evidence that hotel pricing lags guest-perceived quality (Tran, 2027), we pool 453 online reviews of five upscale and upper-upscale hotels in Orlando and Fort Lauderdale, each analyzed in a graduate case study. LIWC scored guests’ Achievement, Affiliation and Power language, and structural equation models related motives and seven guest ratings to perceived value and market revenue. A single quality factor explained guest ratings well (CFI = .959, RMSEA = .086), and Value tracked quality closely (β = .91), with no independent effect of motives or class. Yet the two large Orlando Marriott convention hotels showed a persistent value gap, rating Value about half a point below their other attributes, against about one-tenth of a point at the other three hotels (difference = −0.40, t = −6.17). Within those two hotels the gap did not move with monthly market rates. We interpret this as a sticky rate position: price set for the class tier and held above delivered quality. Managers should reset rate positions when value ratings signal a gap, rather than wait for the next budget cycle.

detail.abstract: Brand measures derived from large language model (LLM) outputs are only useful if they hold still when nothing about the brand has changed. This study reports a pre-registered third wave of the AIAS™ measurement protocol: a verbatim re-acquisition, in November 2026, of five product-category panels (audiophile headphones, skincare, cosmetics, automotive, premium spirits; 112 brand units) first measured in May 2026 (t₁) and re-measured in June 2026 (t₂), on a fixed six-model panel whose dated versions were confirmed identical to t₂ and which begins retiring on 24 November 2026. The t₂→t₃ interval is 152 days. All 852 study calls returned, and four computational-reproducibility gates passed before any t₃ statistic was computed. The per-brand rank order of the v1.8 Consistency instrument φ held over the long horizon (H_Phi_LongHorizon CONFIRMED: pooled ρ = 0.681, n = 80), exceeding both a brand-label permutation null and a pre-registered frame-structure null that scrambles model identity within each question (p_frame = 0.0001; null 95th percentile 0.51). Recall Presence held its order in all five categories (H_Presence_LongHorizon CONFIRMED: ρ = 0.927–0.976). No decay from the three-week to the five-month horizon was detectable for either instrument (H_Horizon_Decay MARGINAL for both; D = +0.019 and +0.002, intervals spanning zero). Changes in Consistency were unrelated to changes in Presence (H_Drift_Dissociation CONFIRMED: ρ = 0.032). Of 58 brands below the recall floor at t₂, 56 remained below it. The results give the two-component AIAS 2.0 construct a long-horizon reliability base and are the last data this model panel can provide.

detail.abstract:
The luxury streetwear market has become an increasingly large part of the global fashion industry in recent years. In order to stand out in a competitive market, many brands use psychological tactics such as exclusivity, limited releases and scarcity. Knowing how these affect consumers and branding will help understand how brands use these tactics. 

This paper explores how brands use tactics like limited releases, exclusivity and collaborations to create scarcity. By looking at how brands like Supreme and Corteiz use these tactics, it shows how they can create interest in consumers. 

This research uses both primary and secondary research to show how scarcity affects brands. The primary research was using a questionnaire with 50 people asking about how they feel about limited releases and other scarcity tactics. The secondary research looked at academic articles, industry reports and case studies. The results suggest that scarcity can help make people want to buy the product more. 74% of respondents said they would be more inclined to want a luxury product because of its limited availability. 90% said the brand would appear more exclusive because of the scarcity. This was however a general question about luxury brands, meaning the findings cannot fully be related to the case studies.

detail.abstract: Previous studies about online review-response tend to quantify correlations of factors at the expense of boxing away the underlying cause-and-effect processes. Based on evidence from multiple sources, this study reveals the causalities in review-response exchanges in tourism: Present exchanges, conditioned by accessibility and a logic of persuasion, can be explained through the working of emotion, judgement, and intentionality; Reviewers' and managers' interactions with their surroundings and with other people generate new social forms, i.e., appreciation, persuasion, and bonding, which contribute to social transformation and reproduction. Causal factors express their powers separately, while individually their expression can strengthen, weaken, or joins up with another mechanism, subject to condition e.g., humangenerated or AI-generated managerial response. The study enhances our understanding of what is in the black box in online review-response exchanges and advocates a morphogenetic framework for guiding future investigations on service review and recovery.

detail.abstract: We examine whether generative artificial intelligence (AI) speeds up software development at the expense of code quality. Our novel monthly panel tracks 1,459 corporate public software projects from 2022 to 2026, covering 3.9 billion lines of source code. An industry-standard tool identifies maintainability issues, bugs, and security vulnerabilities in each monthly snapshot of the code. We convert its estimated repair time into a dollar measure of technical debt, the future cost of resolving maintainability issues. We compare code quality changes around first detected AI use with changes at comparable projects where we have not yet detected AI use. Contrary to concerns about "AI slop," total issues per line decline by 1.4%, bugs per line by 2.1%, and technical debt per line by 0.7% of their averages before detection. Quality gains concentrate in projects with weaker development practices before AI use. We also find that issues per unit of software functionality decline relative to comparison projects. Together, the findings link detected AI use to faster growth in firms' software assets and a lower engineering burden relative to both code volume and software features.

detail.abstract: This paper relates exchange value with non-rivalry and conditional data network effects. Widespread treatment of data like an ordinary, private good creates problems for participants in data trading markets as they give data away to create and capture value. However, the attributes of data call for a different approach that resembles service-dominant logic rather than goods-dominant logic. Without this, both agents and the surrounding ecosystem needlessly lose value. This paper examines an existing data sharing ecosystem that trades genetic data and comprises a data producer, data analyst and an open market. We formally model the effect that supply level and supply frequency have on value created from shared data by agents on both sides of the exchange as they pursue either short- or long-term growth strategies. We demonstrate that a servicedominant view of data enables an expanded Pareto frontier as agents invert the value creation process by sharing value to create data. Additional applications of the model include comments on interactions with ‘generative AI’, vertical integration in data supply chains, reverse subsidies, and quantitative data governance thresholds.

detail.abstract: Many online shops now divide visitors into behavioral clusters and serve each cluster a different interface variant. The usual justification is that clusters group people who respond alike, so a variant chosen for a cluster should work better than a single variant for everyone. This article examines that chain of reasoning. We decompose the value of cluster-specific variant assignment into the gain from true heterogeneity, the loss from assigning users to the wrong group, and the loss from choosing the wrong variant on noisy data. We then propose a validation protocol that treats clustering as a means to an end and judges it by held-out outcomes. A simulation with four latent segments, three interface variants, and a baseline conversion rate near 3 percent shows how little of the available gain standard pipelines capture when cluster separation is moderate. At the highest separation we tested, three standard deviations between segment means in six behavioral features, the best pipeline, k-means with the true number of clusters, raised conversion by 0.048 percentage points over the best single variant. Pipelines that chose the number of clusters by silhouette or Bayesian information criterion gained between 0.000 and 0.020 points at that separation, and at lower separations no pipeline differed clearly 1 from zero. The results argue for held-out outcome validation, for larger samples per cluster than practitioners usually allow, and for a conservative default in which a single interface remains the baseline that any segmentation has to beat.

detail.abstract: Prediction markets rely on a resolution process that converts observed events into contractual payoffs. We study how experiencing a dispute over this process affects subsequent trading on Polymarket. Using 814 matched pairs of disputed and undisputed events and a stacked difference-indifferences design, we find a modest decline in weekly trading activity and a 1.43 percentage-point increase in realized returns on subsequent purchases. Traders reduce purchases in markets with higher settlement risk and increase purchases in lower-risk markets. They also buy later, sell before market close more often, and hold positions for a smaller fraction of a market's life. Mediation analyses show different return associations for these adjustments: later entry is negatively associated with returns, while pre-close selling and a shift toward lower-risk markets are positively associated with returns. Responses vary across dispute types and trader characteristics. An additional market-level analysis finds larger forecast errors in markets with a high share of dispute-experienced traders. The findings show how dispute experience reshapes the timing and allocation of subsequent trading and inform the design of contract rules and resolution processes.

detail.abstract: Most artificial intelligence (AI) tools for health care are built in well-funded hospitals, trained on data from those hospitals, and tested against the staff and equipment those hospitals have. This viewpoint asks what happens when such tools travel to a clinic in Cameroon. It compares two reports by the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) and the National Academy of Medicine (GAO-20-215SP and GAO-21-7SP) with the author's experience in Cameroonian mission and private clinics. Five findings emerge. First, AI recommendations depend on context, and context travels badly. Second, most clinical AI tools GAO reviewed were still being designed or tested. Retraining one for a new site can cost from hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of dollars. Third, the clearest near-term gains are at the front desk: scheduling, reminders for missed visits, and records. Fourth, the safest design sends a patient's concern to a human clinician, not to a machine diagnosis. Fifth, patient safety depends on security from the first day. The author argues that African health systems should build AI around their own staff and workflows from the start. The paper closes with implications for ministries, clinic leaders, universities, and software builders.

detail.abstract: Many firms license their pricing algorithms from third-party providers. We study how ownership in this upstream market shapes algorithm design and downstream welfare. In our model, a continuum of downstream firms faces a common demand shock and can license an affine algorithm, a base price plus a responsiveness to the shock, from either one provider or two. Firms differ in a preference type that providers cannot observe, so they sort across the available algorithms. Competition works in two directions. The competing algorithms respond less to the demand shock, which improves social welfare. But the two providers also differentiate their algorithms more to soften fee competition between them, and the resulting dispersion of base prices around the efficient uniform level reduces it. The second force can dominate when the dispersion ratio lies in an intermediate range and downstream products are poor substitutes, making provider competition lower social welfare. Measured against the two-algorithm menu benchmark, consumer surplus never falls once all firms adopt, so the two welfare standards can disagree. Three extensions locate the mechanism. A single-algorithm monopoly enlarges the welfare disadvantage of duopoly. When heterogeneity is on the cost side rather than the preference side, the same sorting raises welfare. Finally, letting the algorithm partially personalize its base price on the adopter's private preference undoes the over-differentiation: the harm shrinks with the pass-through and vanishes under full personalization, so the welfare-optimal degree of personalization flips with market structure.

detail.abstract: This article examines the European Union's shift from market-based governance towards economic security in the regulation of semiconductor supply chains and their critical raw material base. It argues that recent EU semiconductor policy should not be understood simply as sectoral industrial policy or as a move towards technological autarky. Rather, it reveals a broader transformation in European economic governance, in which resilience and economic security increasingly complement market integration, competition and regulatory harmonisation as organising principles. The article develops the concept of a systemic coordination industry to explain why semiconductors generate governance challenges that cannot be adequately addressed through decentralised market coordination alone. Drawing on qualitative document analysis of the European Chips Act, the Critical Raw Materials Act and the European Economic Security Strategy, the article shows how the EU is extending governance upstream to critical materials, strengthening selected semiconductor capacities and creating horizontal mechanisms for risk coordination. The findings suggest that the EU is not abandoning market governance but adapting it to a geopolitical and technological context in which selected dependencies are treated as systemic risks. The article contributes to debates on European integration, strategic autonomy and industrial policy by conceptualising economic security as a new layer of EU market governance rather than as its replacement.

detail.abstract: AI systems are increasingly relied upon in the judiciary to carry out a variety of tasks (referred to as 'judicial AI') with the aim of improving judicial decision-making. This aim, however, presupposes an underlying normative ideal of what 'good' judicial decision-making is, which can be used to assess whether judicial AI indeed brings judges closer to the ideal. In this article, I seek to advance two goals. First, I articulate an ideal of judicial decision-making that draws on Martha Nussbaum's conception of 'poetic justice' (section 2). This conception not only emphasizes knowledge about the law, but also the importance of some inherently human virtues, which dispose judges to acknowledge the individuality and dignity of the parties involved, rely on their emotions to attain a more comprehensive understanding of the case, and use their imagination. Second, I explore how judicial AI can advance or undermine the ideal of poetic justice (section 3). While traditional AI intuitively runs counter to this ideal, I argue that the responsible deployment of generative AI, which seems more prone to 'poetic' decision-making given its ability to mimic certain human qualities, could actually enhance judges' poetic capabilities, and I offer several examples. At the same time, I also point out important shortcomings and describe how reliance on this technology can undermine poetic justice. My analysis reveals that the impact of generative AI on this ideal cannot conclusively be determined, as much depends on the design, purpose and deployment of the system. I therefore offer some suggestions of how judicial AI can be brought in line with poetic justice (section 4), which serve as pathways for future research, such as acknowledging the sui generis character of judicial judging, adopting a 'frictional' approach to the design and use of judicial AI, and introducing targeted regulation, before concluding (section 5).

detail.abstract: Growing global supply chain complexity has generated interest in multi-tier management, yet most research focuses on focal firm and Tier-1 ties, overlooking Tier-2 dynamics. A specific gap exists in investigating Digital Transformation Initiatives (DTI) within triadic relationships among the focal firm and its Tier-1 and Tier-2 suppliers. This study addresses this gap by utilizing a multiple-case study approach across diverse sectors, drawing on 30 interviews, to examine the diffusion of DTI across multi-tier supply chains, with particular attention to the Double Agency Role (DAR) of Tier-1 suppliers. Using social capital theory and agency theory, our findings emphasize the key role of social capital in the DAR of Tier-1 suppliers. The importance of relational and cognitive capital varies as we shift from downstream to upstream segments of the supply chain. Relational capital is crucial in the downstream segment (focal firm-Tier-1 supplier), while cognitive capital grows in significance as we move upstream (Tier-1-Tier-2 suppliers). Additionally, we create a matrix to illustrate the relationships among social capital, the DAR, and the effectiveness of DTI diffusion. This study contributes to the digital transformation literature by expanding its focus from dyadic to triadic relationships. It also offers practical implications for supply chain managers, providing actionable insights to enhance the diffusion of DTI. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpe.2025.109728

detail.abstract: Two posts can lose visibility in the same feed, yet only one may come with a route to appeal. We examine how recommendation platforms document what creators can challenge, what viewers can change, and which decisions the platforms retain. We use an abductive comparison of archived policies and first-party documentation from TikTok, X, Pinterest, and Snapchat. The sources we reviewed tied appeals to specified enforcement restrictions. We found no comparable route for ordinary lower ranking. The clearest documented remedy restores a post's eligibility for recommendation and leaves subsequent placement and reach open. Viewer controls range from topic preferences to feed-mode choices. They shape selection for the person who uses them, while some enforcement restrictions apply across feed modes. We extend information systems research on control configuration by showing how authority over one decision can constrain a later decision that the platform still controls. For designers and regulators, the findings identify what a 2 safeguard should make verifiable: which decision it addresses, why that decision was made, and what changes when the safeguard is used.

detail.abstract: Merger control typically asks who owns what (the “map”). In a world with AI, that question is too narrow. What firms own says little about what they can do. What matters is the capability to deploy an AI system into production (the “compass”). This paper builds a four-step test that puts this capability at the center of merger analysis and checks it against every merger decision the Commission published through June 2026. The test guards against two errors at once, the clearance won on an asserted capability and the prohibition that never examined a real one.

detail.abstract: We introduce the Horizon Intelligence Quotient (HIQ), a psychometrically principled framework for evaluating articial intelligence systems on probabilistic forecasting tasks. Existing AI benchmarks report accuracy on incommensurable scales, conate task diculty with system capability, and provide no reliability bounds. Drawing on classical psychometric theory and the Brier Skill Score (BSS), HIQ converts raw forecasting performance into a population-normed scale (mean 100, standard deviation 15) via the formula HIQ = 100 + 15(Φ-m)/s, where Φ is the system's BSS and (m, s) are norm parameters estimated by leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV) to avoid circularity. We derive (1) a closed-form standard error SE HIQ = 15/(s √ n) and SpearmanBrown reliability bounds for principled sample-size planning; (2) an analytic contamination correction ∆HIQ = 408δ, where δ is the fraction of benchmark items leaked into training data; (3) a norm-drift estimate of 3.03.75 HIQ points per year for longitudinal comparability; and (4) the Meridian decomposition, which resolves overall HIQ into four orthogonal componentsReach, Efciency, Adaptivity, and Breadthenabling multi-dimensional capability proling invisible to scalar scores. Applying HIQ to ve AI systems from Halawi et al. (2024) via LOO-CV yields scores ranging from 60.1 (Gemini-Pro) to 130.6 (GPT-4-1106-Preview), demonstrating meaningful discrimination across architectures. We release hiq-score, a pure-Python library implementing the full framework with 32 unit tests, together with two empirically estimated pilot norms.

detail.abstract: The Basel Committee and the European Union recognise tokenised traditional assets as eligible collateral on different terms. SCO60.28 to SCO60.30 condition recognition on a positively confirmed comparison with the traditional asset under distressed market conditions and cap eligibility at the CRE22 list; EU law applies general, non-comparative conditions. Where recognition is reached, the haircut is identical. The comparative benchmark has a prudential function: a tokenised asset inherits the haircut of its conventional counterpart, and the benchmark tests whether that calibration can be transferred to it. EU law contains no recognition condition directed to that function. The only specific mandate for technical standards on the EU condition was deleted in 2024, and no comparative application was identified in the supervisory material examined. A worked example shows that, for a standardised-approach loan collateralised exactly at its value under the comprehensive method, without mismatch, non-recognition multiplies risk-based capital by the haircut's reciprocal. The comparison yields four positions: a comparative test in Canada and Hong Kong, conditional parity in the United Kingdom, express parity for tokenised collateral in the United States and, in EU law, parity without any statement on tokenised collateral recognition. The benchmark should be followed; non-recognition may be a disproportionate consequence.

detail.abstract: This study involves an integrative literature review and a process framework explaining the mechanisms to confront and alleviate employee Artificial intelligence (AI) resistance in organizations. First, we conceptualize AI resistance as a three-dimensional concept embodied in employees' fears, inefficacies, and antipathies toward AI. We advance that experiencing mistrust, existential questioning, and technological reflection are key individual mechanisms to confronting AI resistance connected to organizational mechanisms to alleviate AI resistance through the continuous interaction and unfolding of anxiety and introspection. We also explain the alleviation of AI resistance as an organizational process consisting of AI accessibility, human-AI augmentation, and AI-technology legitimation, each of which maps into one of the dimensions in the employee-level confrontation mechanisms. Overall, our conceptual framework provides an overarching and granular understanding of AI resistance, how employees confront it, and how it can be alleviated in the workplace. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.hrmr.2024.101075

detail.abstract: This study takes a fresh approach to explore the mechanisms of foreign direct investment (FDI) spillovers in the context of emerging economy firms, specifically focusing on the Turkish automotive industry. Given emerging economy firms' inherent constraints in R&D and resources, FDI serves as a critical avenue for them to acquire technological and managerial knowledge. While previous literature has extensively analyzed spillovers from an economic perspective, our research introduces a neoinstitutional perspective in organizational sociology to understand how these spillovers manifest and influence productivity and innovation. Importantly, we examine the role of international buyer-supplier relationships, a key aspect in shaping spillover outcomes. In so doing, we draw on rich qualitative data from 7 Turkish direct and sub-suppliers of large automotive multinational enterprises (MNEs). Our findings underscore the significant influence of the institutional context and relational mechanisms on the effectiveness of FDI spillovers, revealing why anticipated positive effects may not always materialize. This study contributes to the existing literature by addressing the limitations of prior research and provides practical insights for policymakers in emerging economies, empowering them to leverage FDI for economic growth and organizational success. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.intman.2026.101340

detail.abstract: When researching the experiences of African minorities as immigrants, using authentic or indigenous methodologies requires a deep understanding of both the socio-cultural dimensions of migration and the exclusionary structures within the marketplace. We highlight how indigenous methodologies can be used to examine four themes: (1) market exclusion and structural barriers (including economic, social, cultural); (2) the use of diverse epistemologies to ensure research on African immigrants incorporates Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) principles and recognizes the legitimacy of multiple ways of knowing; (3) how African immigrants navigate identity through cultural continuity, adaptation, and resistance; and (4) the validation of African immigrants' voices and knowledge by positioning them as central actors in the research. detail.abstract: Stiglitz and Weiss (1981) show how adverse selection can produce credit rationing. This paper examines how sequential, non-exclusive lending can reverse that restraint, producing socially excessive credit ("reverse credit rationing"). A capacity externality arises when additional lending reduces existing lenders' expected recovery. A priority externality arises when a lender attracts repayments at other lenders' expense. Borrowers who can meet all minimum payments but can't pay off every balance in full send additional payments to higher-APR accounts to cut interest costs. Lenders have the incentive to raise rates to attract these payments if early repayment sufficiently improves net expected recovery. This advantage can render loans privately profitable even when their social costs outweigh their benefits. Financial distress can reverse the repayment priority as borrowers protect future access to cheaper credit. Correctives should ensure that new lenders internalize the losses imposed on existing lenders and that then resulting equilibrium generates a socially durable access to beneficial credit avoiding overexposure of borrowers.

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Journal of Logistics Research and Applications, 29(10), 1275-1306. DOI:10.1080/13675567.2025.2540863

detail.abstract: This study analyses the World Bank's Logistics Performance Index (LPI) to quantify changes in logistics performance before and after COVID-19, using a slack-based measurement (SBM) model of data envelopment analysis (DEA) and the Malmquist Index (MI), which indicates efficiency changes over time. The LPI analysis shows performance gains, but challenges in timeliness and international shipments. The SBM-DEA model indicates efficiency improvements mainly through technological advancements. After the pandemic, the decline in efficiency in customs operations and international shipments signals a need for streamlined procedures and cost reductions. The analysis also shows that the post-pandemic recovery varied by region. This study contributes to the theory by showing how dynamic capabilities and institutional resilience influence logistics adaptability and widen global performance gaps. Informed by the resource-based view and dynamic capabilities theory, it advises policymakers to enhance logistics infrastructure, modernise customs, and reduce costs to tackle postpandemic challenges in underperforming regions. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1080/13675567.2025.2540863c

detail.abstract: The leading developers of artificial intelligence (AI) are among the most valuable and influential companies in the world, yet their corporate governance has received little attention in the literature on AI governance. We contribute to filling this gap by comparing the governance of four leading AI firms (OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and Alphabet/Google) and, more briefly, Mistral, Meta and DeepSeek. Two observations stand out. First, the leading AI firms are all closely held or controlled through dual-class shares, which reflects a broader revival of founder control in tech firms. Second, the firms differ sharply in whether and how their stated purpose is protected. OpenAI is controlled by a nonprofit foundation, Anthropic by founders under a purpose trust with the right to elect a majority of the board, Alphabet by founders with conventional checks and balances, and SpaceX by a single founder with few checks. Purpose-protecting devices-public benefit corporation status, foundation control and purpose trusts-are imperfect and must cope with enormous challenges, but from a governance perspective they are a great deal better than complete autarchy (non-governance). The paper concludes that private-law governance arrangements can be a valuable complement to public regulation.

detail.abstract: As industrial business-to-business firms increasingly pursue digital servitization to generate recurring revenues, making digital services commercially viable remains difficult, especially when value capture depends on customer access, data permissions, and intermediary-governed contractual arrangements. Although prior research has emphasized value creation and capability development in digital servitization, we know little about how industrial firms make digital-service pricing commercially viable. In this paper, we undertake a longitudinal exploratory qualitative case study of a leading European OEM operating in a mission-critical context. Our findings make three contributions. First, we develop a pricing-conditions perspective by showing that digital-service pricing depends on data access and interpretability, measurability and attribution, governance positioning, and service architecture and repeatability. Second, we identify four digital-service commercialization patterns of SLA-enhancing, incident-based, predictive, and planning-oriented, and enabling and infrastructural services that explain why digital services differ in how they can be packaged and defended commercially. Third, we develop four pricing configurations, i.e., ad hoc, customized, standardized, and value-based pricing, showing that pricing viability depends less on selecting a pricing approach than on aligning the service's commercial role, customer-value locus, feasibility conditions, and commercial and governance arrangements. In this sense, pricing in digital servitization is better understood as a configurational approach than an isolated price-setting decision and strategy. By doing so, the study extends research on digital servitization and industrial pricing, offering a configurational understanding of how, and under what conditions, digital-service pricing becomes commercially viable. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.indmarman.2026.07.006

title: Assortment Planning and Pricing with Consumer Searching: The Role of Anticipated Regret
affiliations: University of Mannheim - Business School, University of Mannheim - Business School and University of Mannheim - Business School

detail.title: Assortment Planning and Pricing with Consumer Searching: The Role of Anticipated Regret

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: Consumers cannot search all available alternatives before purchase due to limited information-acquisition capacity. Consequently, they typically engage in a "consider-then-choose" process: first forming a consideration set and then searching products within this set to make a purchase decision. We extend assortment and price optimization under consumer choice behavior by incorporating consumer anticipated regret into consideration set formation. Specifically, after purchase, consumers may passively encounter information about unconsidered alternatives. If an unconsidered product turns out to be superior, they may regret having decided on a small consideration set (under-searching regret). If no better alternative is found, they may regret having decided on a large consideration set (over-searching regret). Anticipating such regret, consumers optimally adjust their consideration sets ex ante. We show that anticipated under-searching regret enhances firms' ability to influence consumer choice through assortment decisions, whereas anticipated over-searching regret limits this ability. We also find that to steer consumers toward desired consideration sets, firms may need to offer additional products that consumers will ultimately not consider, which increases the complexity of assortment planning and pricing problems. Even in a homogeneous market, which is the simplest situation, the assortment problem exhibits a structure analogous to a two-dimensional knapsack problem, for which no fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) exists in general. Despite this increased complexity, we develop an FPTAS for the assortment problem with homogeneous consumers and provide an exact mixed integer convex reformulation for the assortment problem with heterogeneous consumers. We further reduce the joint assortment and pricing problem to a finite collection of one-dimensional optimization problems. Our findings identify an additional behavioral rationale for offering products that generate little or no direct revenue. Although these products may not be considered, their presence can influence consumers' anticipated regret and thereby shape consideration-set formation.

detail.abstract: Consciousness research has developed increasingly sophisticated accounts of awareness, integration, access, and reportability, but it remains unclear which observable behaviors should count most as evidence of consciousness. This paper proposes costly agency as a confirming behavioral marker. Costly agency is a freely chosen, externally verifiable act that imposes a real cost on the actor, runs counter to an actor's immediate convenience or interest, is not selected by a present instruction or reward, and serves another party's stake. The proposal extends an earlier Five Cs model into a Seven Cs framework: curiosity, critical thinking, creativity, compassion, conscience, courage, and connection, all grounded in context. The novelty lies not in any individual capacity, each of which has an established research tradition, but in treating their integrated expression under genuine constraint as the relevant unit of behavioral evidence. The paper translates that integration into five tests: costly, self-opposed, unprompted, other-regarding, and verifiable. An illustrative business case shows how the seven capacities can fuse in a consequential choice, and three predictions specify conditions that could count against the account. Applied to machine consciousness, the framework complements indicator-based and behavioral inference approaches by identifying behavior that should carry greater evidential weight than fluent self-report or trained prosocial responses. Costly agency is not presented as necessary for consciousness or as proof of phenomenal experience, but as a testable standard for unusually strong behavioral evidence of integrated conscious agency.

title: Economics of Selection in Ranking & Selection: Neither Fixed-Precision nor Fixed-Budget
affiliations: INSEAD - Technology and Operations Management, National University of Singapore and University of Minnesota - Minneapolis - St. Anthony Falls Laboratory

detail.title: Economics of Selection in Ranking & Selection: Neither Fixed-Precision nor Fixed-Budget

affiliations.org_name: University of Minnesota - Minneapolis - St. Anthony Falls Laboratory

detail.abstract: Ranking and selection (R&S) has evolved tremendously over the last several decades, with applications in agriculture, discrete optimization with computer simulation, clinical trial design, and other areas.We challenge a widely accepted classification of R&S procedures into two categories, fixed precision and fixed budget. We discuss a third class, economics of selection (EoS) procedures, which is conceptually distinct and is found in extant literature on Bayesian hypothesis testing and simulation optimization. Procedures in this third class seek to optimally balance two quantities: the cost of learning about the performance of each alternative and the quality of the alternative that is ultimately selected on the basis of that learning. Fixed precision and fixed budget procedures tend to optimize one of these quantities, while putting a constraint on the other. We clarify these differences and show why it matters. We then present new frequentist R&S procedures in this third category, including both twostage procedures and a sequential heuristic, assuming Gaussian observations that have either known or unknown variances. We find that EoS is not a question of Bayesian or frequentist, nor of asymptotic or finite sample analysis, nor of finite-stage or fully sequential, nor of one mean versus a standard or comparing multiple alternatives. We identify opportunities for further R&S research.

detail.abstract: Over the past decade, several countries have started to implement "co-operative compliance" programs designed to improve the relationship between taxpayers and the tax authority. One key feature of these programs is that taxpayers continuously share tax information with the tax authority. We examine the compliance effects of such information sharing through an experiment involving four treatments: (i) no audits and no information sharing, (ii) audits and no information sharing, (iii) audits and information sharing with a tax consultant, and (iv) audits and information sharing with the tax authority. Our results suggest that the potential for tax audits increases tax compliance, but information sharing with the tax authority does not incrementally enhance compliance. This result is due to two opposing effects: (i) a negative compliance effect induced by motivational crowding and (ii) a positive compliance effect driven by the intrinsic motivation to be honest. When information is shared with a tax consultant, we observe lower tax compliance compared to information sharing with the tax authority and audits only, likely due to moral disengagement through diffusing responsibility. Overall, our study sheds light on the behavioral response of taxpayers to information sharing, informing policy makers deliberating the implementation of cooperative compliance programs.

detail.abstract: Rampant insider trading threatens market integrity and investor confidence. Vindicating the macroeconomic basis of the federal securities laws requires more robust prohibitions and enforcement. This article posits that the reinvigoration of agency fiduciary duties  prohibiting the retention of undisclosed trading profits arising from agency/principal relationships can operate to achieve the macroeconomic goals of the insider trading prohibition and stimulate innovation and macroeconomic growth. Both state and federal law enforcement as well as private litigation should pursue this expanded prohibition and enforcement. Recent empirical evidence fully supports the approach envisioned in this article.

detail.abstract: The accelerating electrification of transport, alongside the growth of decentralized renewable generation, is increasing stress on distribution grids. While electric vehicles (EVs) are often seen as an additional burden, their batteries can be leveraged through Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) to support grid flexibility. However, existing V2G research almost exclusively treats EVs as stationary storage at a single charging location, overlooking their mobility and their potential to deliver V2G services at different nodes throughout the day. This paper compares three V2G strategies of increasing spatial flexibility: Stationary V2G, where each EV operates only at its home node; Locational V2G, where EVs also operate at the nodes they naturally visit during the day; and Relocation-enabled V2G, where a fleet operator repositions vehicles toward the nodes where charging or discharging is most valuable, following location-and time-dependent congestion prices. The strategies are evaluated on two real medium-voltage (MV) grids under summer and winter conditions. Each grid is coupled to a low-voltage (LV) feeder through two coordination directions: in Top-Down, the MV solution is imposed on the LV feeder; in Bottom-Up, the feeder optimizes against both grid signals jointly, with an iterative V2G-power flow loop enforcing LV grid feasibility. Results show that Relocation-enabled V2G reduces maximum MV line loading by up to 25% with respect to a no-EV baseline, whereas Stationary and Locational V2G achieve at most 7%, and that Bottom-Up coordination matches or improves on Top-Down in 9 of the 12 scenarios.

detail.abstract: Presenteeism amid pressing emotional demands in business-to-business (B2B) sales is a prevalent yet underexplored phenomenon. Using PLS-SEM and fsQCA, we investigate whether emotional demands foster salesperson resilience while simultaneously exacerbating voluntary and involuntary presenteeism, both directly and indirectly, under the moderating role of collaborative culture, and identify distinct causal recipes for these two forms of presenteeism. PLS-SEM analysis reveals the nexus of relationships among the ingredients of presenteeism: emotional demands enhance salesperson resilience and directly drive both voluntary and involuntary presenteeism. Salesperson resilience mediates the relationship between emotional demands and voluntary presenteeism, suggesting that resilient salespeople are more likely to engage in voluntary presenteeism. However, it neither influences involuntary presenteeism nor mediates the link between emotional demands and involuntary presenteeism, indicating that resilience may serve as a buffer against involuntary presenteeism and enhance salespeople's agency. Collaborative culture negatively moderates the impact of salesperson resilience on voluntary presenteeism but does not moderate its impact on involuntary presenteeism. Furthermore, the fsQCA analysis reveals distinct causal recipes for both forms of presenteeism, including demographic and contextual factors. These findings deepen our understanding of resilience and presenteeism in B2B sales by incorporating Job Demands-Resources theory and contributions from asymmetric causal modeling. ☆ This article is part of a Special issue entitled: '8th IMM Summit' published in Industrial Marketing Management. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.indmarman.2026.02.011

detail.abstract: Observed performance in knowledge-intensive tasks reflects both genuine effort and substitution of effort to artificial intelligence (AI), neither of which is directly observed. This paper shows that relative substitution of effort to AI is identifiable from observed performance measures. Identification relies on matching tasks where the use of AI is allowed to comparable tasks performed in controlled environments where the use of AI is reliably restricted. As a proof-of-concept, the framework is implemented in a small higher education setting but can be extended to any knowledge-intensive workplace. The results suggest that the use of AI in knowledge-intensive tasks creates a mismatch between observed performance and underlying human capital. This introduces a measurement error in performance, compressing its observed distribution relative to the underlying distribution of human capital, and carrying implications for the design of tasks in environments where effort is unobservable, but performance outcomes depend on the use of AI.

detail.abstract: Consumers often evaluate products knowing neither their performance nor how much that performance will matter in use. Using a Bayesian model of consumer evaluation, we show that resolving either uncertainty can increase overall uncertainty about product value by making the unresolved question more consequential. Because consumers decide how much to rely on the product before its value is fully revealed, this uncertainty amplification can lower the value of adoption. The same mechanism reshapes information search: consumers may optimally begin with information that would not improve the purchase decision on its own but reveals whether the remaining uncertainty is worth resolving. We then analyze implications for firms' information disclosure policy. Disclosure can preserve existing purchases and generate additional sales, but it can also discourage the search needed to recognize a worthwhile purchase. When these losses outweigh additional sales, firms generate greater demand by emphasizing information consumers would acquire anyway than by revealing the other dimension.

detail.abstract: This article reviews the industry 4.0 (I4.0) and circular economy (CE) literature from a global value chain (GVC) perspective. More specifically, it (1) summarizes the empirical findings on the applications of I4.0 and CE practices; (2) explores the previous literature and identifies several future research directions to advance the existing literature. In this respect, the interface between I4.0 and CE research is a relatively young field of inquiry that has been little concerned with developments in GVCs. We systematically review 112 peer-reviewed papers in the field of I4.0 and CE to distill key future research opportunities and trends in the GVC field. We develop three specific conclusions from our literature review. First, GVCs can vary widely within the various forms of I4.0 technologies with the various CE practices. Second, GVC research is underdeveloped with regard to I4.0 and CE. Third, our findings are congruent with previously published studies, which recognize the importance of GVC research that has generated a rich body of knowledge, mainly from a governance perspective in operations management, supply chain management, and international business. Likewise, our study offers promising avenues for future research studies at the intersection of I4.0, CE, and GVCs. Our systematic literature review suggests that there are many opportunities to advance the I4.0 and CE debates in the burgeoning field of GVC. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2022.133621

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the effect of firm strategic marketing ambidexterity (SMA) and industry contingencies on the sales function's relative compensation level within organizations. It draws on longitudinal secondary panel data from two different sources, based on a sample of all business-to-business manufacturing firms with more than 100 salespeople in France across several years, and perform a hierarchical linear model (HLM) analysis. The model, tested on multilevel data, shows that SMA and its interaction with industry munificence and dynamism are significant determinants of the relative compensation of the sales function (RCSF). Results show that innovativeness and marketing resource endowment (two dimensions of SMA) have opposite effects on RCSF. Additionally, different industry contingencies-industry munificence, dynamism, and competitiveness-interact differently with SMA when explaining RCSF. This study highlights the relevance of the sales function in firms' pay practices and advances the understanding of variations in RCSF. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbusres.2022.113545

detail.abstract: Supplier firms in the Global South face compounded risks from political instability that challenge their ability to maintain participation in global value chains (GVCs). While resilience is increasingly acknowledged as a critical capability, it remains unclear how suppliers develop resilience when conventional GVC governance strategies, often grounded in institutional stability, prove insufficient. This gap is especially pronounced in knowledge-intensive service sectors like software development, where codification, coordination, and inter-firm trust are central but often disrupted by political instability. This study examines the resilience of GVC suppliers operating in politically unstable regions of South Asia, particularly India and Pakistan. It focuses on the role of governance mechanisms-such as codification, managing complexity, and supplier capabilities, on supplier resilience. It also investigates how trust moderates these relationships. Drawing on Transaction Cost Economics (TCE) and the Dynamic Capabilities View (DCV), we argue that these governance mechanisms function not only as efficiency enablers but also as dynamic governance adaptations that suppliers actively mobilize to survive and adapt. A quantitative analysis using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was conducted on survey data collected from 100 software firms. The results show that task codification and management of task complexity enhance supplier resilience. It further reveals that trust negatively affects the links between task codification and resilience, challenging the conventional assumption that trust uniformly strengthens GVC relationships. The core theoretical contribution of this study lies in extending TCE and DCV by showing how resilience is enabled through external governance adaptation and by rethinking trust as a conditional, context-dependent mechanism rather than a universal good. The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ibusrev.2025.102465

detail.abstract:
Purpose-This paper aims to focus on the influences of the COVID-19 pandemic on business-to-business (B2B) firms' relationship initiation and customer relationship management in an under-explored and unique context of high-tech industrial microenterprises. The authors analyze the challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic in the specific context of B2B relationship initiation and customer relationship management dynamics by examining Finnish B2B industrial microenterprises. 

Design/methodology/approach-The paper uses exploratory in-depth case studies undertaken in three Finnish industrial microenterprises to analyze the influences of the COVID-19 pandemic on their new business relationship initiation and relationship management with the current customers. 

Findings-The case firms quickly adjusted to the “new normal” and used a number of technological resources, including online meetings and three-dimensional demonstrations, among others. A key reason for this quick adjustment was them being microenterprises. However, despite this, lack of access to customer sites remained a hindrance as their products need to fit certain production processes, which cannot be done without physical visits. Furthermore, the development of trust with new customers, especially those based in emerging markets, was challenging due to the lack of physical meetings and site visits.

Research limitations/implications-The research highlights the challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic to B2B relationships and gives an account of the changing dynamics of relationship initiation and customer relationship management amid technological and societal disruptions. It also highlights the continued role of personal relationships and psychical meetings in such relationships. As such, the research informs B2B research that examines the role of personal relationships in B2B marketing.

Practical implications-The study offers industrial microenterprise executives insights into how to face and tackle COVID-19 driven challenges in B2B customer relationship management and how to integrate technological tools in relationship management practices while understanding where face-to-face meetings are indispensable.

Originality/value-The study demonstrates areas in which virtual tools can and cannot be substitutes for conventional means of B2B relationship initiation and customer relationship management across developed and emerging markets. It also highlights the specificities of industrial microenterprises and their business development and customer relationship management dynamics mechanisms, a research area that has been rather ignored by prior studies.

The full paper is available at https://doi.org/10.1108/IJOA-04-2021-2719

detail.abstract:
Generative Intelligence Optimization and Generative Engine Optimization improve how content answers and appears in AI-mediated queries. We distinguish four cumulative dimensions of touchpoint design: content, structure, machine accessibility and real-time adaptation. We call the fourth Adaptive Touch Optimization (ATO). It uses live journey signals to choose and execute changes in content, layout or calls to action within a touchpoint, and can coordinate subsequent contacts when appropriate.

We connect customer journey research, online experiments, causal marketing and sequential policy learning to specify an objective of incremental, verified conversion. The technical blueprint combines an always-on evidence layer, predictive state and effect estimation, a constrained next-best-action policy and agentic execution of approved variants within a millisecond-scale serving budget. Outcome evidence feeds a separate, versioned policy update process.

We compare five naming alternatives and specify tests against fixed, propensity-based and session-frozen policies. The framework yields five falsifiable propositions and a prospective B2B validation design. Evidence from adjacent deployments establishes component feasibility. The proposed system’s incremental value remains an empirical question.

Generative AI disclosure: OpenAI Codex was used for literature discovery, to draft and revise substantial portions of the manuscript, and to prepare the technical blueprint and architecture diagram. The conceptual starting points were the authors’ Essential manuscript and Uwe Seebacher’s specification of the four-dimensional model.

detail.abstract: Real-world asset (RWA) tokenization gives firms a direct-to-investor financing channel alongside bank lending. Facing competition from this token channel, the bank may adjust its loan rate to retain an optimal share of the firm's financing. We examine how the bank's loan-rate response shapes the firm's financing allocation and token-investor outcomes. We develop a Stackelberg game where a firm finances an expansion project with an uncertain outcome. The bank first sets the loan rate; the firm then allocates its fixed financing requirement between RWA tokens and bank borrowing; and investors decide whether to participate in the token offering. First, we find that token financing matters most when the firm's financing requirement is moderate relative to the capital available from potential token investors. At this intermediate level of token-market depth, the firm raises a larger share through tokens, and investors receive larger shares of expected surplus and successful-project financing payments. Second, greater financing frictions reduce the token financing ratio and investors' share of successful-project payments but can increase participating investors' perceived share of expected surplus. Lastly, near the boundary where token financing remains marginally viable, the token financing and payment ratios approach zero, while participating investors can still expect a significant surplus. Two policy implications follow. Governments should assess token-market depth before broadening investor access, because expanding an already deep market can reduce investors' perceived surplus ratio. Regulators should retain asset verification and standardized disclosure safeguards, recognizing that moderate financing frictions may reduce token-financing volume while improving participating investors' relative expected gains.
